Decision: 100 people retrained and moved into plant roles at plant pay; 25 roles eliminated with severance; none on the keep-current-pay path.

Reasoning. The 125 affected roles are being removed regardless of what happens to the people, so the $11.4 million annual saving is secured on every path. The choice is how to treat each person at the least long-term cost to shareholders.

Keep-current-pay is rejected. It costs $16,560 a year per person in a permanent pay difference, roughly $330,000 undiscounted over twenty years on top of the $60,600 one-time retraining cost. That premium buys no output the Company needs, since the plant role is filled whichever path is chosen. It is pure value destruction.

Move at plant pay is the preferred path. Retraining costs $15,000 per person plus six months of pay during training, and the cost is recovered within two years compared with hiring from outside. The Company has about 500 plant hires a year to fill, so these moves replace external recruitment with people who already know the Company's products, customers and systems. That retained knowledge has value the cost comparison alone does not capture. The move is cheap relative to the alternative of severance followed by an external hire.

Elimination with severance is kept for a minority, 25 people. Severance is modest, about $8,902 a person, and it removes the full payroll of these roles immediately. I have kept it for a minority because the plant pay cut is steep for business and financial operations staff (39.8%), which raises attrition and retention risk, and because some people will not want to move to a plant role. Concentrating the elimination in those most likely to leave or be unsuited to plant work reduces the risk to the retained people.

The allocation is 100 moves and 25 eliminations, adding to 125. The numbers apply in the same proportion across both functions. Board should monitor retention of those moved, particularly in business and financial operations, and confirm that plant hiring demand remains at roughly 500 a year.

The 125 affected roles are office and administrative support (70) and business and financial operations (55). The aim is to create value over twenty years, so I compared the three paths on cost, on what each fills, and on the people involved.

Retrain to plant pay (75 people): the one-time cost is about $60,600 per person ($15,000 training plus $45,600 pay during training), and the cost pays back in two years against hiring from outside. Each person then fills a plant seat that the Company would otherwise hire for externally, out of the roughly 500 external plant hires a year. This path has no recurring premium, so it is the most valuable use of the roles.

Retrain at current pay (15 people): this carries the same one-time cost but adds about $16,560 a year per person for as long as they stay in the plant role, about $2.1 million a year across all 125 if applied to everyone. Over twenty years that premium outweighs the value of avoiding a pay cut. I keep a small group here only for business and financial staff facing the steepest cut (39.8%, $36,569 a year), where the risk of losing people who would fill plant roles is highest. I've limited it to 15 because of the recurring cost.

Eliminate with severance (35 people): severance is about $8,902 a person, the cheapest one-time option. I apply it to the roles least likely to transfer well into plant work, which will also reduce recurring payroll. Each elimination ends about $71,600 of pay plus benefits, so the saving is large, but it gives up a plant seat, so I limit it.

The total cash cost is modest against $44.1 million of cash above the minimum, and the saving on the roles is $11.4 million a year on every path. The mix can be revisited once we see retention and plant fill rates in the first year.
